2tfuaz:351: The 60/40 train/test split with the blinded_history design is the part of the skill-creator source code most worth understanding in depth. This mechanism essentially transplants the standard machine-learning method for preventing overfitting (holdout validation) into the LLM prompt optimization scenario. The improvement model (improve_description) does not know the test set performance and can only adjust the description based on train set failures — this ensures that description improvements are driven by generalization, not by "memorizing questions" on a known eval set. Finally selecting best by test score keeps selection pressure directed at true generalization. The elegance is that it uses a clever "information isolation" mechanism (blinded_history) instead of directly modifying the optimization objective.

wgl55j:230: The choice of Bessel's correction (n-1 sample standard deviation) reflects a deep understanding of the randomness in AI evaluation. When we run 3 evaluations, those 3 results are samples randomly drawn from "all possible outcomes", not the full data. Using the population standard deviation (n) would underestimate true fluctuation — which is dangerous in engineering because it creates a false signal that "the evaluation is very stable". The sample standard deviation (n-1) is more conservative for small samples and gives a wider confidence interval, making it a more honest estimate of uncertainty. When facing randomness in AI output, a conservative estimate is more valuable than an optimistic one, because it prevents prematurely releasing unstable Skills.
